qs.q: Which laboratory test is most widely used as a prognostic tumour marker in lymphoma?
o: Serum C-reactive protein measurement for inflammation
Serum lactate dehydrogenase level as a prognostic marker
Beta-2 microglobulin quantification for tumour burden
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate for systemic disease
qs.e: Serum LDH reflects tumour burden and turnover and is incorporated into prognostic indices such as the International Prognostic Index for lymphoma.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Tumour markers are blood‑based proteins or hormones released by cancer cells or by the body in response to cancer. They aid diagnosis, staging, monitoring response and detecting recurrence, but are never used alone for screening.

sections.p: A tumour marker is a measurable substance, usually a protein, that is produced by malignant cells or by normal cells in reaction to a tumour. Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical context, imaging and histology; markers support but do not replace tissue confirmation.
b: Serum assay (immuno‑assay) is the common method
Elevated levels must be interpreted with pre‑test probability

t.b: Is ovarian epithelial cancer likely? – Markedly raised (>35 U/mL) supports diagnosis, but can be raised in menstruation, endometriosis, pregnancy
Is a germ‑cell tumour or hepatocellular carcinoma present? – High AFP (>500 ng/mL) suggests yolk‑sac tumour or HCC; low levels do not exclude disease
Is choriocarcinoma or trophoblastic disease present? – Elevated β‑hCG (>100 IU/L) is diagnostic; normal levels rule out most trophoblastic tumours
Is colorectal or other adenocarcinoma present? – Rising CEA (>5 ng/mL) helps monitor known disease; normal CEA does not exclude early cancer

sections.p: Markers are incorporated into staging systems (e.g., FIGO for ovarian cancer uses CA‑125). Rising levels often indicate advanced stage or residual disease after surgery.
b: Stage I–IV correlates with increasing marker levels
Serial trends are more informative than a single value

sections.p: Most elevations are due to malignancy, but benign conditions are common, especially in low‑resource settings where infections and inflammatory diseases are prevalent.
b: Epithelial ovarian cancer → CA‑125
Hepatocellular carcinoma, yolk‑sac tumour → AFP
Choriocarcinoma, gestational trophoblastic disease → β‑hCG
Colorectal, pancreatic, gastric adenocarcinoma → CEA
Benign ovarian cysts, endometriosis, pelvic infection → CA‑125
Viral hepatitis, malaria, schistosomiasis → AFP elevation

sections.p: Patients often present with nonspecific symptoms (abdominal pain, weight loss, jaundice). Tumour markers may be ordered after imaging suggests a mass or when a known cancer is being followed.
b: Unexplained ascites → consider CA‑125
Persistent jaundice with pancreatic mass → check CA‑19‑9/CEA

sections.p: Markers complement imaging and histology. Choose a test that answers a specific clinical question; if unavailable, rely on imaging and tissue biopsy.

t.b: Is pancreatic/biliary cancer likely? – High (>37 U/mL) supports diagnosis; normal does not exclude early disease
Is a germ‑cell tumour or lymphoma present? – Elevated LDH suggests high tumour burden or rapid cell turnover
Is a granulosa‑cell tumour suspected? – Raised inhibin B is specific; if assay unavailable, use ultrasound and histology

sections.p: Rapidly rising markers may signal tumour progression, metastasis, or treatment failure. Very high levels can cause paraneoplastic syndromes (e.g., hypercoagulability).
b: Doubling of CA‑125 within weeks → consider recurrence
Sudden AFP rise after resection → possible residual disease

sections.p: Treat the underlying tumour (surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy). Marker trends guide response; supportive care includes managing paraneoplastic effects.
b: Surgery removes primary source, often normalising markers
Platinum‑based chemotherapy for ovarian cancer reduces CA‑125
Anti‑emetics and anticoagulation for paraneoplastic symptoms

sections.p: Serial measurement after treatment detects early recurrence. Lifestyle measures (smoking cessation, hepatitis B vaccination) lower risk of marker‑positive cancers.
b: CA‑125 every 3‑6 months for 2 years post‑ovarian cancer
AFP every 6 months after HCC treatment

sections.p: Benign conditions that raise the same markers can mimic cancer.
b: Endometriosis vs ovarian cancer (CA‑125)
Pregnancy vs choriocarcinoma (β‑hCG)
Acute hepatitis vs HCC (AFP)

sections.p: False‑positive and false‑negative results are common; always interpret in clinical context.
b: CA‑125 normal in early ovarian cancer
CEA normal in early colorectal cancer
AFP can be raised by liver regeneration after malaria

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with rising CA‑125 (possible tumour rupture)
Rapid increase in β‑hCG in a pregnant woman (possible trophoblastic disease)
New jaundice with high AFP (possible hepatocellular carcinoma)

faq.q: Can tumour markers be used for cancer screening?
faq.a: No, because of low specificity; they are used for monitoring known disease.

faq.q: What is the most useful marker for ovarian cancer?
faq.a: CA‑125, mainly for monitoring response and recurrence, not for initial screening.

faq.q: Why might AFP be high in a patient without cancer?
faq.a: Acute viral hepatitis, malaria, or liver regeneration can raise AFP transiently.
